diagnostic_evidence.quote: \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} c \\ d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} ac + bd \\ ad + bc \end{bmatrix}

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed weak inverse formula divides by a^2-b^2. For a=-b (which still satisfies the stated condition a≠b), this denominator is zero, but the element (a,-a) is non-zero and does have a weak inverse in the split-complex ring. Thus the formula does not cover all non-zero elements as claimed.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the condition a≠b by a^2≠b^2 and add the missing separate case a=-b (e.g., weak inverse (1/(4a), -1/(4a))).
issues.overall_effect: The claim that the displayed formulas give weak inverses for all non-zero split-complex numbers is false for elements with a=-b.
issues.title: Split-complex weak inverse formula misses a=-b case
issues.why_classification: A local correction of the stated domain and one extra case repairs the example without changing the ring or its main properties.

issues.failure_explanation: For convolution over the group, the sum should be over u,v with u·v=x. With x=i and u=j, the second index is v=i⊕j, so the term should be a_j b_{i⊕j}, not a_i b_{i⊕j}. The displayed formula factors out a_i and therefore does not define the stated group convolution.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the factor a_i to a_j in the displayed convolution formula.
issues.overall_effect: The example claiming this product is the Z_2^k group-ring product is false; the formula does not compute the convolution that diagonalizes under the Walsh–Hadamard transform.
issues.title: Incorrect XOR-convolution formula in group-ring example
issues.why_classification: A single-index correction fixes the example and restores the intended group-ring construction.

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed equality is for squared Frobenius norms. Since the transformed squared norm satisfies ||\hat B||_F^2 = |c|^2 ||B||_F^2, the error in the original domain must be multiplied by |c|^{-2}, not |c|^{-1}. The theorem as stated is off by a factor of |c|.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the factor |c|^{-1} by |c|^{-2} in the error formula.
issues.overall_effect: The exact error formula in the second Eckart–Young theorem is false; the optimality inequality remains but the stated equality is incorrect.
issues.title: Wrong scaling factor in second Eckart–Young error formula
issues.why_classification: A one-line constant-factor correction fixes the formula while preserving the theorem's optimality conclusion.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: there exists an invertible matrix \(\matM\in\C^{n\times n}\) such that for all \(\va, \vb \in \R^n\), we have \(\va \cdot \vb = \va \Mprod \vb\).
The use of complex numbers is unavoidable. It can be shown that no such real \(\matM\) exists.

issues.failure_explanation: The algorithm promises a real matrix M, but Theorem thm:main only guarantees a complex M, and some tubal rings (e.g., complex numbers, the t-product with DFT) require a complex M. For those rings no real M exists, so the algorithm cannot fulfill its stated output contract.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the output type and initialization of M to \C^{n\times n} (and allow the eigendecomposition matrix S to be complex).
issues.overall_effect: The algorithm fails for all tubal rings whose required matrix M is not real, contradicting its stated guarantee and the main theorem.
issues.title: Algorithm find-M restricts output matrix to be real
issues.why_classification: The algorithmic procedure itself is otherwise unchanged; allowing complex M is a local correction of the output type that restores the promised guarantee.
